Stage 1 · Warm-up

Warm-up

Five moments when you did not understand. Match each one to what went wrong.

Match each situation to the reason you could not follow it.

Then write about the last time this happened to you in English. Then tell your teacher which one happens to you most often. Then tell your partner which one happens to you most often.

1You are on a train and the call keeps stopping.
2The lecturer keeps saying “the literature” and you don’t know what she means.
3You are at a concert and your friend is talking next to you.
4The person on the phone gives you a number in two seconds.
5A form asks for your “next of kin”.
Write it down

Write two sentences about the last time you did not understand something in English. What did you say? Keep it — you will come back to it at the end.

Talk about it
  • Which of the five happens to you most often in English?
  • What do you usually say when it happens — and does it work?
Now speak — ask and answer these questions with a partner.
Answer these two out loud before you go on.

1  When did you last have to fill in a long form?

2  What do you do when somebody speaks too fast on the phone?

Then tell the class the one most surprising thing about your partner.

Stage 3 · Grammar

Saying “I didn’t get that” without saying “What?”

Three different problems. Three different things to say.

Read these four lines from three real conversations.
  • You’re breaking up. Sorry, what was that?
  • Could you repeat that, please, and please could you speak up?
  • What does she mean by ‘the literature’? Please could you explain?
  • Sorry, I’m a bit lost.
Look at the four lines. What is the difference between line 2 and line 3?
Choose the phrase by the problem
The problemWhat you sayWhat you are asking for
I couldn’t hear it
noise, a bad line		Sorry, what did you say?
Could you repeat that, please?
Please could you speak up?
You’re breaking up. · It’s too noisy in here.		the same words again, louder
I heard it but I don’t know the wordWhat do you mean by ‘next of kin’?
Sorry, what does ‘marital status’ mean?
Could you explain that, please?		different words, an explanation
I have lost the threadSorry, I’m a bit lost.
Sorry, I don’t follow.		go back and start again
I want to check I got it rightSo do I need to sign both pages?
Sorry, is that W-R-I-G-H-T?		a yes or a no
softenersSorry, … · Please could you… · Could you possibly…  One softener is enough. Two sounds nervous.

FORM. After Could you and Please could you the verb stays plain: Could you repeat that?, not Could you to repeat.

USE. Match the phrase to the problem. Repeat asks for the same words; explain or What do you mean by…? asks for different words.

“What?” is not wrong English — it is just rude. One word, Sorry, in front of it changes everything.

The same polite frame comes back in Lesson 30 for a problem in a restaurant.

FORM. These are fixed phrases: learn them whole. After Could you / Please could you / Could you possibly the verb is always plain — Could you repeat that, please?, Could you speak up? Never Could you to repeat. In What do you mean by…? the word order is a normal question: do + you + mean.

USE — the choice that matters. If the words were fine but you could not hear them, ask for a repeat: Could you repeat that, please? If you heard them perfectly but one word means nothing to you, asking for a repeat will not help — ask for an explanation: What do you mean by ‘next of kin’? Choosing the wrong one is the commonest problem at this level, and the other person just says the same sentence again, louder.

Politeness. English does the politeness with one small word at the front, not with a special verb form. Sorry, what did you say? is polite. What did you say? on its own is not. Pardon? is short and safe on the phone.

Do not stack softeners: Sorry, please could you possibly perhaps repeat that? One is enough.

You will need the same frame in Lesson 30 to deal with a problem in a restaurant, and in Lesson 36 in a job interview.

Real phrases from the coursebook recording.

Full grammar reference — Asking for clarification

Form

MeaningWhat do you mean by ‘next of kin’? · What does ‘occupation’ mean?
RepetitionCould you say that again, please? · Sorry, I didn’t catch that.
SlowerCould you speak a bit more slowly, please?
CheckingDo I need to fill in this part? · So, is that two words?
SpellingHow do you spell that? · Could you spell that for me?

When and why we use it

  • Ask early. A short question in the first minute is easier than a misunderstanding at the end.
  • Repeat the part you did understand and ask only about the rest: So, the sixth of January — but what time?
  • Sorry once is enough; you do not have to apologise for every question.
  • Confirm at the end by reading the key details back.

Signal words

Sorry? · Pardon? · You’re breaking up. · Let me check…

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • What means ‘occupation’? → What does ‘occupation’ mean?A question needs the auxiliary.
  • Can you repeat again? → Could you say that again?Repeat again says it twice.
  • What do you mean with that? → What do you mean by that?The preposition is by.
  • Please speak slowlier. → Please speak more slowly.Slowly is a long adverb.

Don’t confuse it with

Sorry? asks for a repetition. Sorry. is an apology. The rise in your voice does the work.

Useful language
  • Sorry, what did you say? · Pardon?
  • Could you repeat that, please? · Please could you speak up?
  • You’re breaking up. · It’s too noisy in here.
  • What do you mean by…? · Please could you explain?
  • Sorry, I’m a bit lost. · So do I need to…?
Talk about it
  • In conversation 3 the speaker gives up. Was that the right thing to do?
  • Is it harder to ask someone to repeat, or to admit you don’t know a word?
Write about it
  • In conversation 3 the speaker gives up. Would you have done the same? Write one sentence.
  • Is it harder to ask someone to repeat, or to admit you don’t know a word? Write one sentence.

Stage 7 · Now you · role play + ★ guided writing

Now you

Listen to the call again, then complete a form of your own. Take the call with your teacher, then complete a form of your own. Take the call in pairs, then complete a form of your own.

Useful language — keep this open
  • Booking: I’d like to enrol on… · Is it suitable for beginners? · Do you have any places left?
  • Taking details: Could I have your full name, please? · And your date of birth? · Who’s your next of kin?
  • Not heard: Sorry, could you repeat that? · Please could you speak up? · You’re breaking up.
  • Not understood: What do you mean by…? · Sorry, I’m a bit lost. · Do you mean…?
  • Checking: So do I need to…? · Sorry, is that W-R-I-G-H-T?
1 · Work in pairs. Take a card. Do not show it to your partner.

Student A phones. Student B takes the details and fills in the form. Use at least three phrases from the box — you will need them, because each card hides something the other one has to ask about.

Student A — the caller

Your goal: book a place on a course and find out whether you need anything before you go. You are calling from a bus, so the line is bad. You do not know what “next of kin” means. Invent your own details.

Student B — the office

Your goal: fill in every line of the form. Ask for: full name (spelt), date of birth, occupation, marital status, next of kin. Then say what the caller must do before the course starts. Speak quickly.

Run it once. Do not stop for mistakes.

2 · Swap the cards and do it again.

This is the run that counts. Use two phrases you did not use the first time.

Second time round the office worker should speak faster and use one word the caller will not know.
